strengths: Well-motivated empirical analysis of attention sparsity with clear visualizations and layer-drop ablations demonstrating critical importance of middle layers
Practical training-free retrofit requiring no optimization or retraining, easily applicable to pre-trained models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 benchmarks with systematic variation of sparsity ratios and sequence lengths
Demonstrates generalization to multiple architectures (VGGT and π³) and handles large sequences (>512K tokens)
Thoughtful design choices including separate handling of special tokens (camera/register) shown to be important
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of attention patterns and well-documented experimental results
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core block-sparse attention technique is from prior work (SpargeAttention), with main contribution being application to specific domain rather than methodological innovation

Insufficient justification of design choices: why simple pooling works as well as learned projections (A.2), how hyperparameters τ and ρ were selected, why special tokens need full attention only explained empirically not theoretically
Significant performance degradation at high sparsity (75%): VGGT-S75 shows substantial drops (RRA@5: 0.84→0.57), limiting practical applicability without clear guidance on selection
End-to-end speedups substantially lower than claimed 4×: achieves ~2.7× for 100 frames (Table 1), understating practical limitations in communication
Weak theoretical foundation: sparsity pattern attributed to 'correspondence search' hypothesis without rigorous justification; unclear if universal or dataset-specific; no failure mode analysis
Missing comparisons to alternative acceleration methods (pruning, distillation, other sparse attention variants, simple baselines like resolution reduction)
Incomplete ablations: no individual analysis of CDF vs. sparse ratio contribution, block size sensitivity, or investigation of why learned projections fail
Mask computation overhead not discussed; unclear if savings justify additional computation across different sequence lengths
Reproducibility gaps: hyperparameter selection process, block size justification, and implementation dependencies on SpargeAttention not fully specified

strengths: Well-motivated empirical analysis of attention sparsity in VGGT with clear visualizations and layer-drop ablations showing middle layers are critical
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8+ datasets and multiple tasks (pose estimation, reconstruction, tracking) with varying sequence lengths
Practical training-free approach enabling retrofitting without retraining the backbone model
Demonstrates scalability to 512K+ tokens with >75% sparsity, substantially exceeding prior sparse attention benchmarks
Well-executed engineering adaptation with thoughtful handling of special tokens and dual block-selection criteria (CDF + sparse ratio)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution is applying existing SpargeAttention [39] with straightforward engineering adaptations (special token handling). Claimed advantages over SpargeAttention are engineering trade-offs rather than algorithmic innovations

Overclaimed results: Abstract claims 'comparable task performance' but high-sparsity results show significant degradation (75% sparsity: Real Estate 10K 85→65 AUC, CO3Dv2 90→65 AUC, Tanks&Temples 84.4→56.9 RRA@5). Claims of '4× speedup' only achieved with unacceptable accuracy loss
Large gap between theoretical and measured speedups: Theoretical 4× speedup (75% sparsity) yields only ~2.1× actual speedup with no analysis of why. No memory usage analysis provided

Shallow sparsity analysis: Limited exploration of why sparsity patterns emerge. Hypothesis about 'correspondence search' is speculative. No investigation of scene-dependent variations, architectural components responsible for sparsity, or how sparsity scales with input properties

Insufficient ablations: Missing sensitivity analysis for block size, CDF threshold τ, and sparse ratio ρ. Unexplained finding that learned projections (A.2) provide no improvement. No comparison of alternative block selection strategies
Missing statistical rigor: Single-run results with no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing despite stochastic task nature

Incomplete comparison to related work: Comparisons to Fast3r, CUT3R, FLARE are non-sparse baselines. Unclear if these methods could also be sparsified. No systematic comparison of sparse attention variants
Hyperparameter selection unjustified: Choice of CDF threshold (0.7-0.95) and sparse ratio (0.25-0.75) appears arbitrary without sensitivity analysis or principled justification
Reproducibility concerns: Relies on external SpargeAttention implementation; some details unclear; no code release mentioned

strengths: Well-motivated empirical analysis of attention sparsity patterns with clear layer-drop ablations demonstrating criticality of mid-layers; insights about alignment with geometric correspondences are intuitive and well-illustrated
Practical training-free retrofit approach requiring no backbone retraining; generalizes to both VGGT and π³; kernel-agnostic design enables future integration with improved optimizers

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 benchmarks with extensive scalability tests (512K tokens, 75% sparsity), clear visualization of sparsity-performance tradeoffs, and thorough supplementary ablations
Achieves meaningful practical speedups (2-4×) on realistic multi-view scenarios with 100+ frames, addressing genuine scalability bottleneck in current state-of-the-art models
Clear presentation with effective visualizations; honest reporting of limitations and performance-efficiency tradeoffs; comprehensive supplementary results enable reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applies well-established block-sparse attention techniques from LLM literature to a specific model; uses existing SpargeAttention implementation; block selection via top-k + CDF is straightforward heuristic design without fundamental innovation

Significant performance degradation at high sparsity (75%): CO3Dv2 AUC@30 drops 11%, DTU accuracy degrades 48%; claims of 'comparable performance' are overstated; paper lacks clear guidance on practical sparsity-performance sweet spots

Suboptimal speedup analysis: end-to-end improvements (2-2.5×) substantially lag theoretical gains (4×); minimal speedup at 25 frames limits applicability; interaction between frame count and computational bottlenecks not thoroughly analyzed

Special token handling appears ad-hoc: decision to separately attend to special vs. patch tokens lacks mechanistic justification; this feels like a post-hoc fix rather than principled design; no explanation for why special tokens behave differently

Incomplete analysis of failure modes and generalization: no discussion of scene types/geometries sensitive to sparsification; unclear when method is most/least beneficial; all results positive without critical analysis of limitations

Hyperparameter choices inadequately justified: block sizes (128/64) appear arbitrary with no ablation; CDF/sparsity ratio selection underspecified; learned projection experiment (A.2) only on one dataset, doesn't definitively show better selection strategies don't exist

Limited theoretical understanding: lacks principled explanation for why aggressive sparsification preserves performance; missing analysis of what geometric relationships are most vulnerable to information loss at high sparsity

Incomplete comparisons: no evaluation against other acceleration approaches (pruning, distillation, lower precision); related work dismisses LLM techniques without rigorous demonstration; no memory usage analysis (only speed reported)

strengths: Well-motivated analysis demonstrating that global attention in multi-view transformers exhibits pronounced sparsity patterns, particularly in patch-patch interactions (Section 3 and Figures 3-5)

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 8+ datasets (Real Estate 10K, CO3Dv2, TUM, ScanNet, 7Scenes, NRGBD, ETH3D, DTU, Tanks & Temples) with multiple tasks (pose estimation, pointmap estimation, long-sequence evaluation) showing consistent results
Practical efficiency gains of ~3× speedup at moderate sparsity (50%) while maintaining comparable performance on the original downstream tasks

Thorough ablation studies validating design choices: layer dropout sensitivity (Figure 5), special token handling (Figure A-2), linear projections (Figure A-3), and full layer skip ablations (Figures A-4 to A-5)
Clear presentation with effective architecture diagrams (Figure 2) and comprehensive supplementary results tables (A-2 through A-13) supporting reproducibility
Training-free approach that can be directly applied to existing models without requiring additional optimization or specialized kernels
weaknesses: Limited novelty in the sparsity mechanism: CDF thresholding combined with sparsity ratio selection is a straightforward application of existing sparse attention techniques. No comparison to other sparse attention variants (Linformer, Performer, SparseAttention beyond random masking baseline), limiting understanding of relative merit

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: while the paper observes sparse attention patterns, it provides limited explanation for why they emerge or when they are essential. Section 3 is largely observational rather than explanatory regarding the causal mechanisms

Significant performance degradation at practical-to-high sparsity levels: Figure 7 shows non-negligible drops at 75-80% sparsity; on ETH3D at 75% sparsity, chamfer error approximately doubles (0.2→0.4). Claims of 'acceptable performance' at high sparsity are subjective

Lack of justified hyperparameter selection: No principled procedure for choosing CDF threshold τ and sparsity ratio ρ is provided, nor sensitivity analysis showing robustness to these choices. Different datasets may require different hyperparameters, but this is not discussed

Severe limitations in baseline comparisons: No comparison to orthogonal efficiency approaches (knowledge distillation, pruning, quantization, low-rank approximation). SparseAttention comparison uses random masking rather than an optimized sparse attention baseline. Missing comparisons to recent efficient transformers (Flash Attention, etc.)

Questionable generalization: Method evaluated only on VGGT (with limited results on π³ and MapAnything). No evidence the sparse pattern holds for other multi-view transformer architectures or that the approach generalizes beyond these specific models

Ad-hoc special token handling (Section 4.2): Separation of camera/register tokens from patches lacks principled justification and shows minimal improvement at lower sparsity levels (Figure A-2). Suggests this is a patch rather than a fundamental design choice

Limited theoretical analysis: FLOP reduction is calculated but approximation error is not analyzed. No theoretical guarantees on performance degradation or error bounds. Missing analysis of when sparse patterns are sufficient for downstream tasks

Incomplete hardware evaluation: Timing comparisons lack specification of GPU model, batch size, and other hardware details. No wall-clock time results provided. Sparse attention efficiency varies significantly across hardware without specialized kernels

Experimental gaps: All experiments use the same sparse pattern with no comparison of alternative sparsity selection strategies. Long-sequence experiments use limited subsets (supplementary material). Missing analysis of failure modes and when sparse attention degrades performance

strengths: Comprehensive empirical analysis of global attention sparsity in multi-view geometry transformers with clear visualizations showing concentration on patch-patch interactions (Figures 3-4)
Extensive experimental evaluation across 8 datasets (Real Estate 10K, CO3Dv2, TUM, ScanNet, etc.) and 3 models with detailed supplementary results (Tables A-2 to A-16)
Practical efficiency gains demonstrated: 3x+ speedup while maintaining comparable accuracy at 50-75% sparsity
Thorough ablation studies examining special token handling, learned projections, and layer importance contributions
Reasonable attention block selection strategy combining CDF thresholding with Top-K selection for identifying important blocks
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: block-sparse attention is well-established in literature (SparseAttention, SparsAttention); contribution amounts to applying existing techniques to VGGT based on empirical observation

Weak comparisons to existing sparse attention methods: only limited comparison to SparseAttention baseline (Figure 10), no comparison to Linformer, Reformer, Performer, or other principled sparse approaches
Significant methodological clarity issues: block size not specified, CDF threshold computation not explained, special token handling only in appendix; critical for reproducibility
Misleading 'training-free' claim: method requires pre-computed statistics and thresholds; sensitivity analysis missing
Performance degradation at high sparsity not adequately addressed: Figure 9 shows increasing scatter and errors at 75% sparsity; claims of 'comparable performance' don't uniformly hold
No statistical significance testing provided: no error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests; many reported differences appear within measurement noise
Limited generalizability: only tested on multi-view geometry tasks with specific model families; unclear if sparse patterns apply to other architectures (ViT, DeiT) or domains
Missing task-dependent analysis: method performs differently across tasks and datasets without systematic investigation of when/why sparsification fails
Incomplete results interpretation: unclear which sparsity level represents best accuracy-efficiency tradeoff; task-dependent behavior not thoroughly analyzed
Implementation reproducibility concerns: block size, sparsity ratio selection criteria, and CDF computation not justified; no code availability mentioned

strengths: Clear and well-demonstrated empirical observation that global attention in VGGT is highly sparse with concentration on geometrically meaningful patch interactions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6+ large-scale datasets (Real Estate 10K, CO3Dv2, TUM, ScanNet, ETH3D, NRGBD) with multiple task types and both short and long sequences
Significant practical impact: achieves >3× computational speedup while maintaining comparable task performance across all tested datasets and metrics
Thorough ablation studies validating design choices, including layer importance analysis, special token handling, learned projections, and sensitivity to sparsity ratios
Well-presented work with excellent visualizations of attention patterns and clear logical flow from analysis to method to comprehensive validation
Multiple sparsity selection mechanisms validated, showing robustness and flexibility of the approach
Training-free block selection mechanism that is simple to implement and integrate into existing models
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—block-sparse attention and CDF-based thresholding are well-established techniques; the contribution is primarily empirical validation rather than methodological innovation
Task and architecture-specific approach—sparsity patterns appear optimized for VGGT and multi-view geometry, with unclear generalization to other vision tasks or transformer architectures
Missing comparisons to alternative efficiency techniques (knowledge distillation, pruning, quantization, other sparse attention variants like FlashAttention-2)
Limited theoretical justification for why geometric correspondences lead to these specific sparse attention patterns or why sparse attention suffices for cross-view information flow
Hardware evaluation incomplete—mainly results on H100 GPU; wall-clock time on other hardware (V100, A100, mobile) and memory footprint not evaluated
Implementation complexity understated—requires special handling for different token types (patch vs. special tokens) and data-dependent threshold tuning, limiting true 'training-free' claims
Performance degradation at high sparsity ratios (>75%) unclear how method scales to extreme sparsity needed for edge deployment
Missing analysis of why sparse VGGT sometimes outperforms baseline (surprising results in Fig. 7), long-sequence training costs, and sensitivity to block size choices
